packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
UNVERIFIED IMAGE-ONLY READING: PACKET 06

Isolation: I read this packet's PROMPT.md and viewed only its two supplied images and derivatives made locally from them. I did not consult catalogues, editions, previous readings, web sources, repository files, or proposed identifications. No work or author identification is attempted. I read packet 05 independently before this packet, but it supplied no proposed reading or identification for these images.

Layout survey: The central written strip is upside down in both photographs. Rotating each photograph 180 degrees makes its four narrow columns upright. I call those columns C1-C4 from left to right in the rotated view. They seem to form two pairs separated by a wider central space. The strip has a large blank area below the writing after rotation. The writing is small, brown, densely abbreviated, and accompanied by horizontal ruling and vertical column boundaries. Short phrases and reference-like sequences are underlined in the same general ink color. I do not see a discrete red rubric, large decorated initial, running title, or clear question-heading. Small paragraph-like signs occur. The top lines are partly obscured by the binding/adjacent leaf and abrasion. Some text is present sideways on a separate visible leaf; this has a different orientation and larger script, and I do not treat it as continuation of the central strip. There is also a short sideways note below C4 in image-001; it is not transcribed here. The short underlined items may be lemmata or references within commentary, but the layout alone does not establish that interpretation.

Method: Each full image was first inspected for layout. I then used Pillow transpose(ROTATE_180), which reverses the pixel array without resampling. Native-pixel crops of that rotated array were viewed using original detail. No contrast enhancement, sharpening, OCR, or content generation was used. The two survey PNGs were reduced to 20% solely to see layout; all transcriptions below were attempted from the native crops. Rotation outputs have the same dimensions as the originals: image-001 8688 x 5792 and image-002 8526 x 5404.

Line-label convention: Counts run from the first visible text line at the top of each central-strip column AFTER orientation correction, including damaged partial top lines. They do not include sideways text on the other leaf. Counts are approximate because several top lines merge into the binding edge; y values in the rotated image are supplied for the selected blocks. Abbreviation strokes are represented where feasible with a macron, ꝰ, or ꝫ. Parentheses contain proposed expansions. ? marks uncertainty. No gaps are filled from a presumed text.

Marginal and additional matter: There are small lateral marks and a sideways note, but no marginal text is reliably transcribed. No definite deletion or interlinear insertion was recognized; dense superscripts are mostly abbreviation signs, and I cannot safely classify all of them.

Coverage and limitations: Both full images were inspected, then ten native-scale crops sampled image-001 C2-C4 and image-002 C1-C3. Image-001 C1, image-002 C4, much of the margins, and the separately oriented adjacent-leaf writing remain unread. The absence of a rubric meant selecting underlined item openings and surrounding prose instead. Multiple regions were tested rather than stopping at the first faded line. This reading remains highly incomplete: image pixels are adequate to show many pen strokes, but I cannot confidently decode the dense cursive abbreviations. The numerous [illegible] tags represent the reader's unresolved glyphs as well as physical loss; they do not imply that all these areas are physically erased. These snippets are not sufficient by themselves for a reliable source match, and weak word groups must not be treated as established readings. A specialist familiar with this abbreviation system should revisit the saved native crops. Wider photographs alone are unlikely to remedy that limitation. No author, work, date, or provenance is inferred.
